name: Mahāmudrā (the great seal) in the Kagyu

definitions.definition: The nature of one's own mind — empty, luminous, unborn, beyond speech and thought — which 'seals' all phenomena; at once the ground (mind's nature), the path (recognizing and sustaining it through the guru's pointing-out, śamatha–vipaśyanā and the four yogas) and the fruit (the dharmakāya). 'Though Mahāmudrā cannot be shown…' (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v1).
The Mahāmudrā of the amulet box: ground, path and fruit enclosed together; the three self-liberations.

relations.note: the Nāth/haṭha 'mahāmudrā' and sahaja absorption share words, not the Buddhist view of emptiness
Mahāmudrā's mind-nature is the sūtra 'luminous mind' as recognized in meditation

notes: Distinct from prc:mahamudra (the haṭha seal) and the U28/U21 senses of trm:mahamudra.

name: Sūtra, mantra and essence Mahāmudrā

definitions.definition: A later Kagyu classification of approaches to Mahāmudrā: sūtra Mahāmudrā (introduced through the pāramitā path, the Ratnagotravibhāga and the guru's blessing, without tantric empowerment), mantra Mahāmudrā (reached through empowerment and the two stages, including the six yogas), and essence Mahāmudrā (direct pointing-out of mind's nature to a ripe disciple, beyond either). The scheme answers the question raised by Gampopa's practice of teaching Mahāmudrā apart from tantra.

relations.note: the critique that motivated the classification

notes: The threefold terminology is associated with Jamgön Kongtrul and later Karma Kagyu teachers (recent systematization); its earlier history is not certain here.

name: Ordinary mind (tha mal gyi shes pa)

definitions.definition: Present awareness left just as it is — uncontrived, unspoiled by conceptions — which is the dharmakāya when recognized; 'the great way of the ordinary'.

relations.note: ordinary mind is the co-emergent mind recognized

definitions.definition: Mind-as-such co-emergent is the dharmakāya; appearances co-emergent are the light of the dharmakāya; thoughts co-emergent are the waves of the dharmakāya: the instruction joins the disciple to what was never separate.

relations.note: the Buddhist innate (U44) as taught in the Kagyu instruction

definitions.definition: lhan cig skyes pa, the co-emergent: the dharmakāya inseparable from mind, appearances and thoughts; 'co-emergent wisdom, clarity-emptiness free of grasping' (Karṇatantravajrapada).

name: The nature of thought is dharmakāya

definitions.definition: Thoughts are not obstacles to be suppressed: their essence is the dharmakāya, 'nothing whatever, yet arising as anything' (Dorje Chang Thungma); like clouds they dissolve in space when mind is seen (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v10).

relations.note: śamatha calms thoughts; this view recognizes them

definitions.definition: Mind's nature is described as inseparable clarity and emptiness (gsal stong), appearances as appearance-emptiness (snang stong, 'like a moon in water'), the experience of the method path as bliss-emptiness (bde stong), awareness as awareness-emptiness (rig stong).

name: The three and four kāyas in the Kagyu

definitions.definition: Mind itself, unborn and empty, is the dharmakāya; its unceasing clear radiance the nirmāṇakāya; baseless great bliss, union, the saṃbhogakāya (Karṇatantravajrapada); their inseparability the svābhāvikakāya. Death, bardo and birth are brought onto the path as the three kāyas (bka' dpe phyi ma).

relations.note: death–dharmakāya, bardo–saṃbhogakāya, birth–nirmāṇakāya (the text's own correlation)
the tantric reading of the sūtra doctrine of buddha-bodies

definitions.definition: The 'cause' of awakening present in all beings, for three reasons (the dharmakāya pervades, suchness is undifferentiated, the potential is present) — Jewel Ornament ch.1; identified by Nāropa with the luminous mind obscured by adventitious stains, and by the 3rd Karmapa with mind's clarity-emptiness.
Within the Karma Kagyu read both as empty of own-nature (the 8th Karmapa) and as empty only of what is other (the shentong reading of the 8th Situ and Jamgön Kongtrul): not yet reconciled.

Mind itself is clear light: clear because it is awareness, non-conceptual because self-awareness does not conceptualize itself (Nāropa); 'as the sun's essence cannot be obscured by aeons of darkness, so the clear-light essence of mind cannot be obscured by aeons of saṃsāra' (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā v12).

Nāropa's View in Brief: conventionally all phenomena are self-aware mind; ultimately that mind, examined, is beyond existence, non-existence, both and neither; their union is appearance-emptiness like a moon in water.
Kagyu masters teach that 'appearances are mind' (3rd Karmapa; Nāropa's conventional truth) but add that mind is empty; Nāropa criticizes mind-only proponents who take non-dual mind as truly real.

The 3rd Karmapa distinguishes the eight consciousnesses from the five wisdoms into which they transform when recognized (all-ground → mirror-like; afflicted mind → equality; mental → discriminating; five senses → all-accomplishing; with dharmadhātu wisdom).

name: Consciousness and wisdom (rnam shes / ye shes)

definitions.definition: Consciousness is dualistic knowing under delusion; wisdom is the same knowing recognizing its nature; the path does not replace one with the other but reveals the latter in the former.

name: Stillness, movement and awareness (gnas 'gyu rig gsum)

definitions.definition: The three aspects examined in Mahāmudrā vipaśyanā: the mind at rest, the mind moving as thought, and the awareness that knows both; seeing that they are not different is the recognition of mind's nature.

name: Bliss, clarity and non-thought (the three experiences)

definitions.definition: The typical meditative experiences (nyams) of one-pointedness; clinging to them leads to rebirth in the desire, form and formless realms respectively.

Passing meditative experiences are distinguished from stable realization; experiences are to be treated as 'neither good nor bad' (Milarepa to Gampopa); only realization marks the yogas. The ḍākinī's question to Nāropa — words or meaning? — turns on the same distinction.

name: Deliberate and effortless mindfulness

definitions.definition: Mindfulness in Mahāmudrā begins as deliberate, effortful attention and matures into an effortless mindfulness inseparable from awareness itself.

notes: Recalled from Mahāmudrā manuals in substance; locators not known.

definitions.definition: Śamatha with and then without support settles the mind; vipaśyanā looks directly at the settled and moving mind to recognize its nature; the two are finally united in the four yogas.

relations.note: the Kagyu form of the common Buddhist pair

name: The vajra body (channels, winds and drops) in the Kagyu

definitions.definition: The body abides as channels (rtsa), winds (rlung), drops (thig le/bodhicitta) and the five enlightenments, with the mind as great wisdom dwelling in it (bka' dpe phyi ma); the central channel with left and right channels and four wheels; its formation from confusion is set out in the 3rd Karmapa's Profound Inner Meaning and Yangönpa's Hidden Description.

members: rtsa (channels): dbu ma, rkyang ma, ro ma

relations.note: Buddhist form of the channel system

name: The Six Yogas (Six Dharmas) of Nāropa

definitions.definition: Inner heat, illusory body, dream, clear light, intermediate state and transference (with 'entering another's body' and, in some lists, the consort practice) — gathered by Tilopa from four Indian transmissions and given by Nāropa to Marpa; the Kagyu 'path of method'. Lists vary between sources: Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa treats transference and grong 'jug together; the Karṇatantravajrapada adds karmamudrā.
Niguma's six dharmas, a parallel set with the same six topics, taught in the Shangpa.

members: las kyi phyag rgya (karmamudrā; some lists)

relations.note: parallel sets from two ḍākinī lineages; the Shangpa insists on their distinct transmission

name: The four transmissions of Tilopa (bka' babs bzhi)

definitions.definition: Tilopa received the six dharmas from four Indian sources: inner heat from Caryāpa, illusory body and clear light from Nāgārjuna, dream from Lavapa, and intermediate state and transference from Sukhasiddhi (Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa); other Kagyu lists assign them differently (e.g. adding Kukkuripa or the Hevajra/Guhyasamāja/Mahāmāyā/Cakrasaṃvara tantras).

notes: The attribution list is from the local Tōh 2330 (U44's source); variant lists from memory.

name: The path of method and the path of liberation

definitions.definition: The Kagyu path has two streams: the path of method (thabs lam) — the six yogas on the basis of empowerment — and the path of liberation (grol lam) — Mahāmudrā; they are practised together, inner heat being 'the main trunk' and Mahāmudrā the 'illuminator of wisdom'.

The bardo of birth-and-death (this life), the bardo of dream, and the bardo of becoming; in each, clear light, illusory body and union are to be recognized; inner heat and illusory body are trained in the first, dream in the second, and the clear light at death in the third.

relations.note: the Abhidharma intermediate existence is only between death and rebirth

definitions.definition: bar do: counted as three in the Nāropa texts (birth-death, dream, becoming); the being of the bardo of becoming, seeing its future parents, should regard them as the guru and block rebirth or choose it (Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa).

Senses and elements dissolve (form into sound … earth into water … into consciousness); consciousness dissolves into appearance (sign: moonrise / smoke), appearance into increase (sunrise / lamp), increase into attainment (darkness), attainment into clear light (dawn, a cloudless sky); the eighty conceptions cease and white, red and mind meet.

name: The three appearances (appearance, increase, attainment)

definitions.definition: snang ba, mched pa, thob pa: the three subtle 'appearances' or 'empties' through which consciousness dissolves into clear light at death, sleep and in completion-stage yoga.

notes: The Guhyasamāja (U44) framework; recorded here as used in the Nāropa texts.

definitions.definition: At death the ground clear light ('mother') arises; the clear light recognized in practice ('child') meets it, and for the sharpest faculties this is dharmakāya buddhahood.

name: The five clear lights and their five times

definitions.definition: Clear light is natural, of wisdom, of samādhi, of suchness and of realization; it arises at death, in the central channel, in sleep, when equipoise and post-equipoise are one taste, and at insight (bka' dpe phyi ma).

name: The learner's and the non-learner's union

definitions.definition: Arising from clear light, the body of union is the learner's union while the clear-light fire still purifies tendencies, and the non-learner's union when nothing remains to purify — the fruit.

name: The similes of illusion

definitions.definition: Illusory-body training uses the similes of illusion — mirror image, rainbow, moon in water, dream, magic show, bubble, conjuring, mirage, city of gandharvas, echo — the 'twelve similes' in Tilopa's and the ḍākinī texts.

notes: The texts say 'twelve similes'; only the ones named in the local texts are listed.

name: Blending and transference (bsre 'pho)

definitions.definition: A Marpa-lineage name for the six-yoga system: blending (bsre ba) states — day and night, sleep and death, dream and illusory body — and transference ('pho ba); 'the five blendings' are carried onto the path in the bardo.

notes: The designation bsre 'pho for the Ngok tradition is from memory.

name: Buddhahood in one life and one body

definitions.definition: The diligent can awaken in this very life (bka' dpe phyi ma: 'the instruction for the diligent to awaken in this life'; Karṇatantravajrapada: 'no doubt it gives buddhahood in this life'); Milarepa is the exemplar.

name: The four yogas of Mahāmudrā

definitions.definition: One-pointedness (rtse gcig), simplicity (spros bral), one taste (ro gcig) and non-meditation (sgom med), each lesser, middling and greater — twelve levels; each marked by realization rather than passing experience.

members: ro gcig (one taste) — lesser, middling, greater

relations.note: correlations with the paths and grounds differ between Kagyu masters (dsp:four-yogas-and-the-grounds)

definitions.definition: The fourfold frame of instruction: beyond grasper and grasped is the king of views; without distraction the king of meditations; without effort the king of conduct; without hope and fear the fruit is manifest (Gaṅgā Mahāmudrā); a correct view makes meditation and conduct reach the fruit (Nāropa).

name: Ground, path and fruition in Mahāmudrā

definitions.definition: The ground of purification is mind itself, clarity-emptiness; the purifier is the vajra yoga of Mahāmudrā; the purified are adventitious stains; the fruit is the stainless dharmakāya.
Nāropa: the one mind is 'known as ground, path and fruit' and as 'the three tantras of cause, method and fruit'.
That the mind turn to the Dharma, the Dharma become the path, the path clarify confusion, and confusion dawn as wisdom — the whole path in four lines.

name: The six topics of the Jewel Ornament

definitions.definition: Cause (buddha-nature), basis (precious human life), condition (spiritual friend), method (instructions), result (the kāyas), activity (non-conceptual benefit of beings).

Persons differ: what is medicine for the gradual is poison for the simultaneous and vice versa; the simultaneous way is for those with prior training, the gradual for beginners (Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa). The Kagyu manuals likewise alternate analytical and resting meditation according to the student.

name: The eight freedoms and ten endowments

definitions.definition: The precious human life free of the eight unfree states (hells, pretas, animals, long-lived gods, barbarians, wrong views, times without a buddha, impaired faculties) and endowed with five personal and five circumstantial endowments.

relations.note: the Mahāyāna elaboration of the rarity of human birth

name: The four thoughts that turn the mind

definitions.definition: The precious human life, death and impermanence, the cause and effect of karma, and the faults of saṃsāra; contemplated first (Jewel Ornament ch.2–6; the common preliminaries).

name: The preliminaries (ngöndro)

definitions.definition: The common preliminaries (the four thoughts) and the four special ones — refuge with prostrations and bodhicitta, Vajrasattva purification, maṇḍala offering, guru yoga — each usually accumulated a hundred thousand times before Mahāmudrā instruction.

notes: Shared with U45; this is the Kagyu definition.

name: The fivefold Mahāmudrā (phyag chen lnga ldan)

definitions.definition: Mahāmudrā practised with five parts: bodhicitta, the body of the yidam, devotion to the guru, the Mahāmudrā view, and dedication/aspiration — Jigten Sumgön's and Phagmodrupa's teaching, also transmitted in the Drukpa.
All the Buddha's teachings share one intent, and no vehicle's teaching is to be rejected: the premise of Jigten Sumgön's vajra statements.
One in essence, differing in aspect (Gongchig).
To be kept distinct, each with its own ritual and rules (Sakya Paṇḍita).

Devotion is the head of meditation: realization of Mahāmudrā comes through the guru's blessing received with devotion; the guru is regarded as Vajradhara; the qualified guru has the three trainings and experience; Marpa's prostration to the deity rather than the guru is told as a warning; seeing mind directly is 'the guru's kindness'.

The Kagyu lives dramatize it as trial and devotion: Tilopa and Nāropa's twelve hardships, Marpa and Milarepa's towers; the disciple needs faith, diligence, wisdom and compassion; instructions given without the root guru's consent bear no fruit.
The guru tests the disciple's devotion and purifies his karma through ordeals (Tilopa–Nāropa, Marpa–Milarepa); the disciple examines the guru for the three trainings and experience.

name: The four kinds of spiritual friend (Jewel Ornament)

definitions.definition: An ordinary person as spiritual friend for beginners; a bodhisattva on the grounds; a nirmāṇakāya buddha; a saṃbhogakāya buddha — each suited to the disciple's stage.

The guru's direct introduction to the nature of mind, given when the disciple is ripe — Tilopa's sandal on Nāropa's face; the 9th Karmapa's stages: mind in stillness and movement, appearances as mind, mind as empty, emptiness as spontaneously present and self-liberated.
The guru is the root of blessing, the yidam the root of accomplishment, the ḍākinī and protector the root of activity; for the Kagyu, the guru is placed above the deity (Marpa's lesson).

Instructions passed orally 'from mouth to ear', originating with Vajradhara and the ḍākinīs, through Tilopa, Nāropa and Marpa; sealed for thirteen generations (Karṇatantravajrapada); later branches: the Rechung, Ngendzong and Dakpo hearing lineages.

The succession of realized masters — Vajradhara, Tilopa, Nāropa, Marpa, Milarepa, Gampopa and the masters of each school — supplicated as a 'golden rosary' because each is held to have realized the teaching before passing it on.
The instructions are sealed: not to be given to unfit vessels ('the white lioness's milk'); breaking the seal breaks the pledge; the method path is 'sealed three times'.
Kept by practising the guru's instruction continuously 'like a river'; broken by giving the secret instructions to unfit vessels.

name: Recognized reincarnation (the tulku system)

definitions.definition: By the tradition's account the Karmapas are the first recognized line of reincarnate teachers: Karma Pakshi as the rebirth of Düsum Khyenpa, Rangjung Dorje recognized by Orgyenpa; Karmapas are said to leave letters predicting their rebirth.

notes: Scholars often date the first formal recognition to Rangjung Dorje; tradition to Karma Pakshi (both recorded).

name: The black crown of the Karmapa

definitions.definition: A crown said to be woven by ḍākinīs from their hair and offered to Düsum Khyenpa, visible only to the pure; a material replica given by the Yongle emperor to the 5th Karmapa is worn in the black-crown ceremony (the tradition's account).

name: The four great and eight lesser Kagyu schools

definitions.definition: Four great schools founded by disciples of Gampopa and his nephew — Karma, Tsalpa, Barom, Phagdru — and eight lesser founded by disciples of Phagmodrupa — Drikung, Drukpa, Taklung, Trophu, Martsang, Yelpa, Yazang, Shugseb. 'Great' and 'lesser' refer to the generation of origin, not to size.

name: The seven jewels of the Shangpa

definitions.definition: Vajradhara, Niguma, Khyungpo Naljor, Mokchokpa, Kyergangpa, Nyentön and Sangye Tönpa — the single-line (gcig brgyud) transmission of the first generations, after which the Shangpa spread.

The Kagyu's self-description as a lineage of practice and realization rather than of scholastic explanation (bshad brgyud); the Tibetan 'eight great chariots of the practice lineages' count the Marpa Kagyu and the Shangpa Kagyu separately.

name: The union of the Kadam and Mahāmudrā streams

definitions.definition: Gampopa joined the Kadam graded path and monastic discipline with Milarepa's Mahāmudrā and six yogas ('the two streams mixed'); the Jewel Ornament is its textual form.

name: The union of Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen

definitions.definition: Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen are of one essence and may be practised together (3rd Karmapa's Karma Nyingthig; Karma Chagmé; Tselé Natsok Rangdröl).

notes: Nyingma masters also compare them; distinctions insisted on by either side are recorded in U45.

name: The 'white self-sufficient remedy' (dkar po chig thub)

definitions.definition: Recognizing mind's nature is by itself sufficient for awakening (Gampopa, Lama Zhang).
A revival of the Chinese Hashang's view, rejected by Sakya Paṇḍita.
Do not recall, do not imagine, do not think, do not examine, do not control, rest — the instruction for resting the mind in its own place.

name: Powers and signs in the Kagyu (and the warnings)

definitions.definition: Miracles in dream or waking become path if known as illusion and obstacles if taken as real; when the siddhis are attained obstacles become friends of the path (bka' dpe phyi ma); Milarepa displays powers only to teach; Milarepa tells Gampopa that his visions are neither good nor bad.

relations.note: the Kagyu warning corresponds to the general warning that powers are obstacles when grasped

name: The madman's conduct (smyon pa'i spyod pa)

definitions.definition: Conduct beyond convention for the realized — 'practise the conduct of a madman in the great charnel ground' (Tilopa's Acintya) — embodied in the Kagyu 'divine madmen' Tsangnyön Heruka and Drukpa Kunley; not for beginners.

Realization is expressed in spontaneous songs continuing the Indian dohās — Tilopa's and Saraha's songs, Milarepa's Hundred Thousand Songs, the Kagyu Gurtso; the song is itself a teaching and a transmission.
Carrying the guru, the deity and illusion onto the path in all circumstances.
Inner heat, illusory body, dream, clear light, transference and bardo as taught by Niguma — the root of the Shangpa's five golden dharmas.

name: The Mahāmudrā of the amulet box

definitions.definition: Niguma's Mahāmudrā: ground, path and fruit enclosed like the two halves of an amulet box; the three self-liberations; the four faults self-liberated; the four kāyas.

name: The five golden dharmas of the Shangpa

definitions.definition: Pictured as a tree: root — Niguma's six dharmas; trunk — the Amulet Mahāmudrā; branches — the three integrations; flowers — the white and red Khecarī; fruit — the deathless body and mind.
The fruit of the five golden dharmas: a mind that does not die and a body that does not err, i.e. realization of the undying nature; practised through wind and deity yogas (restricted).

name: The six cycles of equal taste (Drukpa)

definitions.definition: Thoughts, afflictions, gods and demons, suffering, illness and death carried onto the path as of one taste.
Non-virtuous, virtuous and unmoving actions and their results (Jewel Ornament ch.6); Milarepa's life shows grave evil karma purified by remorse, ordeals and practice.
The six realms and their sufferings (Jewel Ornament ch.5); clinging to bliss, clarity and non-thought in meditation leads to the desire, form and formless realms (Moonbeams).

In the Nāropa texts the elements are known through their dissolution: earth into water, water into fire, fire into wind, wind into consciousness at death and in yoga; inner heat does not progress unless the 'equal taste of the four elements' is known.

The perfection of wisdom realizes the selflessness of persons and of phenomena (Jewel Ornament ch.17); Nāropa counts the tīrthikas' self and primordial nature among the views of those deluded about their own mind.
